title: The mustard seed
hookLine: bring a mustard seed from a house where no one has died; there is no such house

lines: THE HARD TRUTH, OR THE SOFT DODGE.
cards: Kisa Gotami stands at the edge of a crowd, her little boy on her hip, asking the Buddha for medicine. Everyone else has laughed or looked away. What is there to say to her?
Two answers come easily. The hard truth: he's gone, and that's that. Or the soft evasion: let's not talk about it.
The Buddha does neither. The story says he looks at her and answers yes. You did well to come here.
I know a medicine. But you'll need to fetch one thing for it.

teach.h: A MUSTARD SEED, FROM ANY HOUSE.
teach.b: Go into the city, he tells her, and bring me a mustard seed. In the story, mustard seed is an everyday thing; any house would have it.
But it must come from a house where no one has ever died. Kisa Gotami is overjoyed. She goes to the first door.
Do you have a mustard seed? Of course, they say, and bring it. Has anyone died in this house?
They look at her strangely. What are you asking? The living here are few.

teach.h: THE LIVING ARE FEW, THE DEAD MANY.
teach.b: The dead are many. A grandfather. A sister.
A baby, years ago. The next door is the same, and the next. Every house would gladly give her the seed.
Not one can give it to her the way she needs it. Somewhere along that street, the story says, it comes to her. It isn't only my son.
Death isn't a curse that singled me out. It's in every house in this city. So she carries her son to the cremation ground, lays him down, and lets him go.
Then she comes back to the Buddha, empty-handed. Did you bring the mustard seed, he asks. And she answers, in effect: I don't need it anymore.

The story says she asked to become a nun, and in time she became fully awakened. The Buddha didn't argue with her grief, or lecture. He gave her something to do, and let the city teach her what no sentence could.
It was the walk, and what the walk showed her: death had come to every house.

how: The mustard seed story is told in Buddhist sermons and at funerals, as a way of seeing that loss touches every family.

o: a farmer's wife who planted the first rice field
a mother sent for a seed from a house without death
a healer who made medicine from mustard seeds

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: in every kitchen, easy to give
from a house where no one has died
where she laid her son down
the walk, and what it showed her

s: the Buddha told Kisa Gotami there was no medicine
he said yes, and sent her for a mustard seed.
every house would give her a seed
but not one was a house where no one had died.
the story says she became fully awakened in time.

games.q: a grieving mother asks you for medicine for her dead son. what do you do?
o: tell her plainly that he is gone.
send her to fetch a mustard seed from a house where no one has died.
games.why: the Buddha sends her door to door. every house has the seed, and every house has known death. the city teaches her.

practice: If there's a loss you carry, bring it gently to mind; if not, choose one from long ago. Picture your street, your building, your town, and behind each door someone who has lost someone: a parent, a friend, a pet, a child.
Let the picture widen, city after city, house after house, the way Kisa Gotami found it, and breathe with all of them.

wordCard.voice: Kisa Gotami. The grieving mother who carried her dead son from door to door, searching for a house that mustard seed could prove had never known death.

carryVoice: Your line: no house is untouched. Every door had a seed to give, and a loss to tell. Day seventy-five, done.

sources.ref: Dhammapada commentary, on verse 114; Therigatha commentary on Kisa Gotami
